results.summary: This design is a competition entry for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene, producing a VGA output and audio PWM signal. It is intended to be connected to a VGA PMOD for 640x480 video and an audio PMOD for sound. The design uses HardCaml and operates at 25.25 MHz, with a test mode pin. The documentation is minimal, providing only pinouts and external hardware requirements, so the visual and audio content is not described.

This project is a resubmission of a TinyFPGA design for Tiny Tapeout 8, implemented in Verilog. It provides four inputs, two command pins, and eight outputs, and is configured and then observed via the outputs. No special external hardware is required, and the design includes tests. The documentation is very brief, so the exact function of the FPGA configuration is not detailed.

This Verilog design takes two sensor inputs and a reset, and outputs two signals intended for motors or buzzers. It compares each sensor value against a threshold and, if only one side is active, sends a signal to the opposite motor; if both are active, it sends a signal to both motors. Testing involves driving the sensor pins with 0 or 1 and reading the outputs; a reset pin clears all outputs. External hardware includes ultrasonic sensors, a microcontroller, and haptic motors.

This design implements the Tractive System Active Light (TSAL) function for a Formula SAE electric vehicle, as required by FSAE rule EV.5.9. It reads a 12-bit value from an external AD7476A ADC via a serial interface and compares it to a threshold; if below the threshold, it drives a green LED continuously, and if above, it flashes a red LED at 4 Hz. Testing requires a PMOD AD1 and simulation for at least one second to verify blink timing. The design is intended to be hard-wired in the vehicle and uses a Tiny Tapeout chip for the digital logic.

This is an 8-bit calculator design originating from a ChipCraft lab exercise. It is implemented in Verilog and tested using Makerchip simulation. No external hardware is required, and all pins are marked unused in the provided pin list. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a one-line description and a note about simulation testing.

This is a factory test module designed to verify all I/O pins of a Tiny Tapeout ASIC. It has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, or outputting an 8-bit counter on both outputs and bidirectional pins. The mode is selected by the reset and select pins. It is used during manufacturing test to confirm connectivity and functionality of every pin.

This Verilog design uses a rotary encoder to control a ring of 12 WS2812B LEDs. Rotating the encoder selects which LED is lit, and a button inverts the LED state. The user can select the color (green, red, or blue) via three input pins and set the intensity with two additional pins. The chip outputs a WS2812B serial data stream on one pin to drive the LED chain, and it also outputs the current count value. External hardware includes a rotary encoder and a WS2812B LED ring.

This design generates a scrolling pixelated cityscape video signal for VGA output. The terrain layers are produced using an LFSR to create deterministic randomness. It requires a Tiny VGA carrier board and a 25.18 MHz clock to display 640x480 video. Silicon testing confirmed it works and produces a Tetris-like scrolling display.

This 2x2 tile design is a USB to UART/SPI/I2C/JTAG/GPIO adapter implemented in Gatery. It enumerates as a USB CDC device on a host computer and can bit-bang various serial protocols to communicate with external devices. Testing involves connecting a device such as an LIS2DH12 sensor and running example software. An external 1.5k pull-up resistor on USB_DP is required for USB operation. The design is notable for supporting many protocols on a single chip.

This Verilog design implements a temporal adder, where addition is performed over time with an enable signal. It takes 8 input bits and produces 8 output bits, and is intended to be used as a coprocessor for vector calculations driven by an RP2040. The design was tested using cocotb. No external hardware is required beyond the driving microcontroller.
